notes:
I've written notes for all 38 verses below. Two things are missing:

- **Differences between Protestant traditions:** I found none on this chapter. Where commentators disagree, it's over dates and places, not doctrine, and each side of those disputes includes writers from several traditions.
- **Prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching:** none of the pages I read covered it, so I left that part out.

**About the sources.** Where a quote is credited to someone in brackets, such as "(Knapp)" or "(Wiseman)", it is quoted inside David Guzik's Enduring Word commentary. A few points come only from the Chinese edition of that commentary (chinese.enduringword.com), because the English page I read was cut short. Some verse 5 comments are compiled on a StudyLight verse page.

---

### 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**Overview (whole chapter)**
- Guzik: a good king in the south ends in tragedy, while five unstable, evil rulers in the north follow one another in quick succession. Each evil and each eventually assassinated. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-15/
- Matthew Henry: five kings of Israel follow one another, and all of whom, except one, went down slain to the pit, and their murderers were their successors. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm
- Pulpit Commentary: the writer squeezes seven reigns, nearly seventy years, into one chapter. Chronicles fills in what Kings leaves out. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- Paul Apple (quoted at Precept Austin) calls it a "kingdom sandwich": five wicked kings of Israel between two fairly good reigns in Judah. Precept Austin says to study the chapter alongside 2 Chronicles 26. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-15-commentary

**v. 1**
- Azariah means "Yahweh has helped" and Uzziah means "Yahweh is my strength." Kings often had a birth name and a throne name, and Precept Austin says we can't be sure which is which. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-15-commentary
- Wiersbe takes Azariah as his given name and Uzziah as the throne name he took at 16. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-15-commentary
- Knapp suggests the people chose him directly, not in the way of ordinary succession. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-15/
- Wesley reads "to reign" as meaning to rule solely and fully to exercise his regal power. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-kings/
- The dating is disputed; see Section 3.

**v. 2**
- Pulpit: Chronicles and Josephus confirm the figures. Josephus says he reigned 52 years and died at 68. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- Precept Austin: the 52 years include a co-regency. Only Manasseh reigned longer in Judah. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-15-commentary
- Matthew Henry: Kings records the ages of Judah's kings but not Israel's, which he calls honour God would put upon the kings of the house of David. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: Josephus praises him even more strongly, and 2 Chronicles 26:5 says he sought God in Zechariah's days. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- Matthew Henry: it was happy for the kingdom that a good reign was a long one. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm

**v. 4**
- Matthew Henry: he lacked the zeal and courage to remove the high places. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm
- Patterson and Austel see in this a basic spiritual shallowness that the eighth-century prophets would expose. Trapp says it lessened his "crown of glory." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-15/
- A gentler view (Restoration Commentary): Azariah didn't realise the high places were a sin, because no one had taught him better. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/2-kings-15.html

**v. 5**
- All the commentators I read explain the leprosy from 2 Chronicles 26:16–21: he took the priest's role and burned incense in the temple.
  - Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/15-5.html
  - Wesley: https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-kings/
  - Poole: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/2_kings/15.htm
- Guzik: he broke the principle that no one should combine the offices of king and priest (and prophet) until the Messiah came. Knapp says that by law the penalty was death (Numbers 18:7), and leprosy was a living death, prolonged and intensified. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-15/
- Matthew Henry: he was probably repentant and forgiven, but stayed leprous as a warning to others, and perhaps for his own soul's good. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm
- Constable: few people stay spiritually strong once they reach worldly success. Like Solomon, Azariah's early success proved his undoing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/15-5.html
- Pulpit on the "separate house":
  - It was probably a house standing alone, perhaps built for him. There is no evidence that Israel had hospitals.
  - Jotham ran the royal palace and did the king's work, of which "judging" was one of the highest duties.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- Pulpit and Precept Austin both report Josephus's version: an earthquake split the temple roof, and a ray of sunlight struck the king's face, bringing on the leprosy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-15-commentary
- Smith: Uzziah stayed king even while leprous, with Jotham acting for him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/15-5.html
- Elmer Martens (quoted at Precept Austin): the Hebrew word covers a wider range of skin diseases than modern "leprosy." https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-15-commentary

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: for his main deeds (his wars, building and army), read 2 Chronicles 26. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- A Bible Hub article: Kings leaving out the cause of the leprosy is about narrative focus, not a contradiction with Chronicles. https://biblehub.com/q/why_omit_azariah's_leprosy_cause_here.htm

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: Chronicles adds that he was buried in the field around the royal tombs, not in the tomb itself, because lepers were unclean. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- Guzik: Uzziah's death is the setting of Isaiah's call (Isaiah 6:1). Isaiah had reason to be discouraged, but he saw the LORD enthroned, greater than any earthly king. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-15/

**v. 8**
- Wesley: the throne had stood empty for several years because of internal strife. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-kings/
- Knapp: there is a gap of about 11 years, during which there was probably anarchy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-15/
- Pulpit rejects any such gap; see Section 3.

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: this is the standard formula. In six months Zechariah could do little good or evil. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- Matthew Henry: these rival kings quarrelled with each other but agreed on keeping up idolatry. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm

**v. 10**
- Guzik: Zechariah was so despised that Shallum could kill him publicly. This ended Jehu's dynasty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-15/
- Wiseman: of the six rulers in Israel's last twenty years, only one died naturally. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-15/
- Pulpit: Josephus calls Shallum Zechariah's "friend." The phrase "before the people" is unusual (see Section 3). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: this is the usual closing formula. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html

**v. 12**
- Pulpit:
  - The promise of four generations also implied the dynasty would last no longer.
  - It ties this to Hosea 1:4 and Amos 7:9.
  - By breaking from David's house, Israel had sown the seeds of its own instability.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- Matthew Henry: See how punctual God is to his promises. The disasters were held back until that word had been fully kept. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm

**v. 13**
- Guzik: Jehu's dynasty lasted four generations, Shallum's four weeks. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-15/
- Wesley: That dominion seldom lasts long, which is founded in blood and falsehood. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-kings/
- Pulpit: "a month of days" means thirty days, according to Josephus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: Josephus says Menahem was the army's general and that Shallum fell in a battle. Tirzah was the earlier royal city. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- Grant: Those who grasp after power are very soon left powerless. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-kings-15.html

**v. 15**
- Guzik: the writer passes no moral verdict on Shallum, perhaps because he reigned too briefly. The violence of his rise and fall shows he lacked God's blessing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-15/

**v. 16**
- Guzik: this atrocity shows how brutal and godless the times had become. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-15/
- Wiseman: Israel was copying a practice that Aram, Ammon and Assyria had used against Israel. https://chinese.enduringword.com/2-kings-15/
- Poole: Menahem did it to frighten everyone else into obeying him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/2_kings/15.htm
- Pulpit: it may not have broken the war customs of the day, however much he transgressed the laws of humanity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- Where Tiphsah was is disputed; see Section 3.

**vv. 17–18**
- Pulpit: the writer treats Menahem as no better or worse than the kings before him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- Wiersbe calls Menahem the cruellest of the five. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-15-commentary

**v. 19**
- Guzik: Menahem bought Assyrian backing, which began Israel's dangerous dependence on Assyria. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-15/
- Matthew Henry:
  - Menahem trusted his own people so little that he paid for peace.
  - The easy plunder encouraged Assyria to come back.
  - So the man who should have protected his country betrayed it.
  - https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm
- JFB: Pul is the first Assyrian king named in the Bible after Nimrod. It links this to Hosea 5:13: "Ephraim [Israel] went to the Assyrian". https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm

**v. 20**
- Pulpit: 1,000 talents at 50 shekels a head means about 60,000 men were taxed. Its homiletic notes add that much of this wealth had been squeezed from the poor, and the burden probably fell back on them in the end. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- A quote in Guzik notes that the rich bore the tax, but Amos and Micah show how they had gained their wealth. https://chinese.enduringword.com/2-kings-15/
- Pulpit: Assyrian kings usually went home after each campaign. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html

**vv. 21–22**
- Pulpit: nothing more is known of Menahem. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- Catholic Encyclopedia: Menahem seems to have died a natural death. https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/tce/m/manahem.html

**vv. 23–24**
- Pulpit: his reign did nothing worth recording. Josephus says he was as cruel as his father, but that may be only a guess from how short the reign was. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html

**v. 25**
- Pulpit:
  - Josephus says Pekah was a "captain of a thousand" and killed Pekahiah at a feast.
  - "Citadel" means the highest tower of the palace.
  - Argob and Arieh were probably the king's friends who died with him, not Pekah's fellow plotters.
  - The Greek Old Testament (LXX) reads "fifty men of the Four Hundred," probably the royal bodyguard.
  - Pekah seems to have acted from plain ambition.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- Patterson and Austel: the plot came from the king's own bodyguard (my translation of the Chinese edition). https://chinese.enduringword.com/2-kings-15/

**vv. 27–28**
- Guzik: the dynasties kept changing, yet there was an amazing continuity of evil. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-15/
- Matthew Henry: Pekah became a great terror to Judah (Isaiah 7:1). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm

**v. 29**
- Guzik: Pekah's anti-Assyrian policy backfired. This was the first major deportation and a sign that Israel was becoming a vassal state. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-15/
- Pulpit links this to 1 Chronicles 5:26, the exile of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- JFB: Tiglath-pileser's annals describing this campaign have been found at Nimrud. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm

**v. 30**
- Guzik: another king and dynasty end by assassination. https://chinese.enduringword.com/2-kings-15/
- The date "twentieth year of Jotham" is disputed; see Section 3.

**v. 31**
- Pulpit: Pekah's reign was important but is told very briefly. Chronicles adds his defeat of Ahaz (2 Chronicles 28:6). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html

**vv. 32–33**
- JFB and Wesley: he was 25 when he began to reign alone, having ruled before as his father's deputy.
  - JFB: https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm
  - Wesley: https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-kings/
- Pulpit: Jotham's 16 years probably include the regency, so he may have reigned alone only five or six years. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- Matthew Henry: Jotham died at 41, too great a blessing to be continued long to such an unworthy people. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm

**v. 34**
- Pulpit: Jotham learned from his father's example and "prepared his ways" before God (2 Chronicles 27:6). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- Matthew Henry: Josephus describes him as pious, just and lacking no princely virtue. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm
- Knapp: since Saul, Jotham is the only Hebrew king with no recorded failing. https://chinese.enduringword.com/2-kings-15/

**v. 35**
- Guzik and Knapp: Jotham built the gate to link palace and temple, keeping his "line of communication" open with God. Guzik contrasts this with his father, who misunderstood that link and grabbed priestly power. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-15/
- Wesley: it was a gate of one of the courts of the temple, probably that which led to the king's palace. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-kings/
- Pulpit: the "higher gate" was probably on the north side, and fortifying it suggests fear of attack from that direction. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html

**v. 36**
- Pulpit: the main event of his reign was the war with Ammon (2 Chronicles 27:5). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html

**v. 37**
- Matthew Henry: the attackers meant wrong, yet God sent them, as with Shimei and Job. Men are God's hand—the sword, the rod in his hand. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm
- Pulpit: these punishments came from the people's inner corruption. They began under Jotham and grew under Ahaz. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- Guzik: this was only "a beginning." God would watch how Judah responded to correction. https://chinese.enduringword.com/2-kings-15/

**v. 38**
- Pulpit: his full name may have been Jehoahaz. "Ahaz" ("possession") is an unlikely name for a godly father like Jotham to give. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html

---

### 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

I found no real doctrinal split on this chapter. Commentators from different traditions agree on the main points: the leprosy was a judgment on pride, the end of Jehu's dynasty fulfilled God's word, and God sent Rezin and Pekah. The tradition labels below are my own descriptions of the writers. The pages I read say only that Benson was a Wesleyan/Methodist Arminian.

The real disagreements are over dates and places, and they cut across traditions:
- **v. 8, a gap before Zechariah's reign?** Wesley (Methodist) says the throne was empty for several years. Pulpit (Anglican-era) says such a gap is not to be thought of.
  - Wesley: https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-kings/
  - Pulpit: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- **v. 16, where was Tiphsah?**
  - Gill (Baptist) puts it near Samaria, citing Bunting's estimate of six miles away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/15-16.htm
  - JFB (Scottish Presbyterian/Anglican) and Pulpit say Thapsacus on the Euphrates. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm
  - Benson (Wesleyan) leaves both open. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/15-16.html
- **v. 30, "twentieth year of Jotham":** see Section 3.

---

### 3. Other views

**Chronology (vv. 1, 8, 13, 23, 30)**
- Pulpit says the numbers clash. It thinks "twenty-seventh" in v. 1 should read "fifteenth," and Shallum's real start was probably Uzziah's 27th year. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- Precept Austin instead solves it with a co-regency: Azariah ruled with his father from about 792 BC and alone from about 767 BC, which was Jeroboam's 27th year. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-15-commentary
- On v. 30:
  - Pulpit thinks the text is probably corrupt, since v. 33 gives Jotham only 16 years. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
  - Wesley takes it as 20 years from the start of Jotham's reign, which is the 4th year of Ahaz. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-kings/
  - JFB: the writer dated it by Jotham because he hadn't yet introduced Ahaz. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ki/2Ki_015.cfm

**Text of v. 10**
- Pulpit: the Greek (LXX) translators didn't understand "before the people" and produced a name, "Keblaam." Ewald proposed an invented king, "Zobolam." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html

**Assyrian records (vv. 19–20, 29)**
- Bible Odyssey (modern scholarship): Menahem paid tribute to Tiglath-pileser III in his first western campaign. "Pul" is that king's Babylonian throne name. https://blog.bibleodyssey.org/dictionary/menahem/
- Pulpit agrees, and notes that Tiglath-pileser's own records list tribute from "Minikhimmi of Samaria." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-15.html
- An older view, Poole: he identified Pul with "Pulbelochus" of ancient historians. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/2_kings/15.htm
- ISBE (on the NET Bible site): Tiglath-pileser's annals name five Hebrew kings, including Azariah, Menahem and Pekah. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=Tiglath-pileser
- Hastings' Dictionary:
  - The towns of v. 29 aren't preserved in the annals.
  - Pekah saved his land from further harm by paying tribute.
  - https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hdb/t/tiglath-pileser.html

**Catholic readings**
- Catholic Encyclopedia on Ozias (Uzziah):
  - The name "Azarias" in Kings is probably a copyist's error.
  - Uzziah appears in Christ's family line (Matthew 1:8–9).
  - https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/11379a.htm
- Catholic Encyclopedia on Menahem:
  - His reign matters because Assyria first entered Israel's land then.
  - Pul is Tiglath-pileser III.
  - Pro-Assyrian factions may have invited the Assyrians in (Hosea 7:11).
  - https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/tce/m/manahem.html
